processing: A strong blend of fully oxidised black teas, usually the maltiest Assam and darkest African teas available, in broken and CTC grades; some versions add a little Keemun or a smoky Chinese black for depth. Blended to a fixed house taste.
harvest_season: Not a harvest: blended year-round and rebalanced each season to stay constant.
appearance_dry: Dark, small, even leaf and granules; loose versions show heavy black Assam leaf.
taste_profile: The strongest of the breakfast family: dense, malty and woody with a dark, slightly smoky or cocoa-like depth and a heavy tannic finish that needs milk.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, 4–5 minutes, milk. Sellers say it was blended for Scotland's soft water, and it does come out gentler with soft or filtered water and harsher with hard; if your water is hard, cut the steep to 3 minutes.

vintage_note: No vintage and no harvest year: a year-round blend with a two- to three-year best-before, sold loose by tea merchants and in bags by a few supermarket brands. Recipes vary, since there is no settled definition; some lean on Assam and Kenya alone, others add Ceylon for brightness or a touch of Chinese black for smoke. Read the origin list, and expect loose blends to be noticeably rounder than the bags.
description:
Scottish Breakfast is a heavyweight among the breakfast blends: usually darker and maltier than English Breakfast, built on strong Assam and African teas and sometimes finished with a little Chinese black for a smoky undertone. The story that it was blended to suit Scotland's soft water is repeated by many sellers, but its origin is not documented.

Like all breakfast teas it is a recipe rather than a tea, mixed to a constant house taste and adjusted with every season's crop. It comes in loose orthodox form and in CTC bags, and the two are quite different in weight and roughness.

Brewed hard, four or five minutes with boiling water, it gives a nearly black cup that is thick, malty, woody and tannic, and it is made to carry milk and a heavy breakfast. In hard water it can turn harsh and dull; filtered water and a slightly shorter steep bring it back into balance.

There is no vintage and no fixed definition, so blends differ widely; the back of the pack tells you whether it is Assam and Kenya alone or something with Ceylon and China in it. Buy loose for the rounder version, bags for speed.

If you want to taste the parts, a plain Assam and a plain Kenyan black side by side show the backbone, and a drop of Lapsang Souchong in a pot of English Breakfast gets you close to the smokier style.
history:
Scottish Breakfast is one of the common breakfast blends, alongside English and Irish: robust, full-bodied black teas often drunk with milk. Little is documented about who first sold it or when.

Sellers often say it was blended to suit Scotland's soft water, but that remains a trade story rather than an established fact. With no fixed recipe, it is defined mainly by each blender's idea of a stronger breakfast tea.
